newsitem.title: USA: Mass. lottery sales slow; profit growth up 81 pct.
newsitem.headline: Mass. lottery sales slow; profit growth up 81 pct.

text.p: Massachusetts state Treasurer Joe Malone Wednesday said cuts in operating expenses at the state lottery are increasing the amount the lottery returns to cities and towns even though lottery sales growth is down.

Malone told State House News Service the new accounting technology and payroll reductions have lowered operating costs to the point where those costs are just 2.2 percent of gross sales - the lowest cost-to-sales ratio in the country.
Malone said that when he took over as treasurer, operating expenses were 4.1 percent of sales.
Sam DePhillippo, director of the $3 billion-a year lottery, said sales are expected to show a 5.8 percent increase this fiscal year, down from an 8.4 percent increase in fiscal 1996.

"It's the long-term impact of not actively promoting the product through traditional methods," said DePhillippo, whose ad budget was reduced to $400,000 from $11 million by legislators in the early 1990s.
The two provided a breakdown of what happens to the average lottery dollar:
60 to 70 cents are returned to wagerers in prize money.
23 to 33 cents goes to the state general fund and local
aid.
Five percent goes to the agents who sell lottery tickets.
Two percent goes to the Lottery Commission.

Still, he and Malone said, the lottery will net $700 million this year, an increase of $38 million over last year, driven by both the sales growth and the reduction in expenses. They said the multi-state Big Game has captured some legal-gambling dollars that previously were wagered out-of-state on Powerball.
The pair said recent bad publicity seems to have had no impact on lottery sales.
News stories in recent months have suggested lottery administrators flouted the legislative cap on their advertising budget by issuing millions in coupons for free or discounted tickets.

And the state auditor recently issued a report saying the administration appears to have set up a special, hidden fund for entertainment and lottery promotion, to skirt legislative constraints on spending.
Despite the bad press, "My sense is that people have a very favorable rating toward the lottery," Malone said, adding about 65 percent of adult Bay Staters play the game.
He said he is constantly trying to strike a balance between a healthy lottery that increases local aid, and "tugging at people's shirtsleeves" urging them to gamble.
That is why the lottery commission now supports a rollback of Keno, a highly popular - and addictive - video numbers game.
The Government Regulations Committee is preparing a bill that will limit the places where Keno can be installed, and restrict the Lottery Commission's power to issue and revoke agents' licenses.
Malone said the game was "somewhat out of control" in its early days, with some convenience and package stores becoming de facto casinos.
